Of course my right hon friend always upholds the rules of the house.
I have seconded this amendment, Mr Speaker, and that is my justification for taking part in this debate before the motion comes to a vote. As a general principle I believe everyone will agree that confidence is the bond which must exist between governments and those they rule. Confidence is what gives strength and success to their undertakings; confidence is the mainspring, the breath of life of governments, and without it no legislative, administrative or executive act of a government can carry any weight.
Especially is this so at a time of trouble and unparalleled difficulty. To-day many nations are fighting depression and ruin. Peoples with their backs to the wall have been attempting new and startling experiments. In his address the right hon. gentleman referred to President Roosevelt of the United States having been given dictatorial powers much greater than those which the House of Commons has conferred upon the Prime Minister. He forgets, however, this vital and fundamental difference between the two cases. Have you noticed, Mr. Speaker, that in every country where unprecedented powers have been granted leaders, whether it be in Italy, in Germany or in the United States, those leaders have behind them the solid support of the country. Do you believe that President Roosevelt would have been able to enlist what appears to be the unanimous support of the United States in the great initiatives he has taken in order to fight the depression in the United States if he had not had behind him the support of that nation? Opinions may differ as to whether he will succeed, but everyone agrees that he is fighting courageously and that he has the confidence of the masses in the policies he is trying to carry out, because he has proved himself independent of all controlling interests whether social or financial and because he is fighting the battle of the people. He has created a spirit, a state of mind and a national will in his country to try to come out of the abyss. He acts; he has done something, and even that is better than paralyzing inactivity.
In Ottawa, unfortunately, confidence is lacking, and without it nothing efficient can be done. The ship of state does not move.

The government in Ontario exists only because it has extended its life for a number of years longer than the electors had in mind when electing it to power. The result in one by-election, namely that in East Kent, shows the trend of public opinion in the province of Ontario.
In his address the right hon. gentleman opposite suggested that defeat is the fate of all governments in times of depression. Well, it is not the fate of the government in the province of Quebec. In that province quite recently there have been three by-elections. One was contested and the Liberal candidate was elected by an increased majority. The two others were unopposed. One vacancy was in the constituency of Jacques Cartier, a constituency which in this house is represented by the general organizer of the Tory party in the province of Quebec. speechtext:
Yes, wait and see. That is the great cry for victory in every battle. Hon. gentlemen coming from my province know that in every instance federal issues were discussed. Their friends bitterly resented those discussions in the by-elections.
The Prime Minister and his government have been on trial everywhere, in every part of the country, in every agricultural, industrial and mining constituency throughout Canada. East and west, north and south there has been a united verdict. I have too great personal admiration for the right hon. gentleman leading the government-and he knows it-to believe for one moment that he will force himself upon an unwilling country, despite the advice he receives from those around and behind him. Let him not be deceived 'by the cheers with which he is acclaimed and by the interruptions with which I am received when speaking. The most powerful force in the consolidation and support behind my right hon. friend opposite in this House of Commons is the terror of a dissolution. Their cheers, and my right hon. friend knows it, have the same value as the musical expressions of those timorous people who sing when they pass a cemetery.
I have this further to say: Some people appear to be under a delusion that when a

The Address-Mr. Lapointe

government is elected for five years it must go to the limit of its term. The other day the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) stated that his reason for opposing the amendment is that this house was elected for a term of five years, and that it must go to the limit of its term of office. Last week one of the newspapers of my own city in a well written editorial took the same stand, and said that the Prime Minister must not mind the demands for a dissolution, that he had been elected for five years and that he should stay for that length of time. This is a mistake. The American constitution provides for the election of a president for a fixed number of years. The British or Canadian cabinet has no such term of office. Its life depends on the confidence of the people and the country. It is in direct violation of the principles of our constitution that a parliament should continue its existence when it no longer commands the support or enjoys the confidence of the majority of the people. This government to-day is in as humiliating a position as was the Conservative government, or whatever its name was, in 1921. At that time all the by-elections had gone against the government when my right hon. leader moved an amendment to the address similar to the one we are now discussing. On that occasion I quoted statements of British statesmen and British constitutional authorities in support of the views I have just expressed. Time does not permit me to quote all of them in this debate, so I shall refer to only one or two. When Mr. Gladstone had dissolved parliament before the expiration of his term of office because of the fact that by-elections had gone against him, and when he had been reproached in the British House of Commons for having taken such action he said:
I think he-[DOT]
Meaning the gentleman who had spoken.

fundamentally misunderstands the constitution of this country if he supposes that the actual majority that a government may possess in an existing House of Commons is sufficient to give it more moral and political strength for the discharge of its arduous duties, after it has become apparent or when it is becoming clear that the possession of that majority is not agreeable to the sense and the convictions of the country.
And he added:
. . . and the mere possession of a parliamentary majority, satisfactory as it is when it is a true indication of the actual current of feeling and opinion of the country, is no adequate support and no adequate warrant for the continuance of a government in office if it has become clear, or when there is reasonable
[Mr- Lapointe.]
ground for supposing that the desires of the country are in an opposite direction.
Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman in 1905 took the same stand. At that time his remarks were:
The moment the House of Commons gets out of touch and harmony with the country, then that plea for retaining office dissolves; and the right hon. gentleman has no right to entrench himself behind the confidence and support of his friends here after it is known to all mankind anid to himself, as well as to any of them, that he has lost the confidence of the country.
I should like to quote Professor Dicey in his Law of the Constitution and what Sir William Anson says in his Law and Custom of the Constitution, but if any hon. gentlemen would like to see those quotations I would refer them to the Hansard of 1921, page 464 and following pages.
We are moving this amendment because it is the right and the duty of the opposition to protect as far as it can the constitutional doctrine of the responsibility of parliament to public opinion. The Prime Minister has lost the confidence of the country largely because of his unredeemed pledges, his broken promises, and the facility with which those promises were repudiated by one who had represented himself in 1930 as having found the key to an earthly paradise. I shall not refer to those promises as they have been quoted quite frequently in this house, but one cannot help remarking the singular similarity between the way the right hon. gentleman emphasized those pledges and the way Herr Hitler in Germany speaks to his people. The Prime Minister used to finish his sentences by saying, "or I will perish in the attempt." Hitler, in his momentous address to the German people on the eve of the so-called elections a few months ago used the following language, "If I fail, hang me to the gallows." Mr. Speaker, we are not cruel on this side of the house and the only thing we want to hang my right hon. friend with is the ballot boxes of the electors of Canada.
The public distrust which is shown everywhere in the country is largely" due to the failure of all the policies which have been initiated by this government, and which have almost ruined our trade and made our agriculture destitute. At every meeting where it was my privilege to speak, either at by-elections or elsewhere, I have asked the friends of this government to name a single one of its policies which has been successful. At last one of the ministers seemed to take up the cudgels and discussed at length the reduction of the expenditure of the Canadian National Railway. What a tremendous achievement!

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
The trade policies of hon. gentlemen opposite have inflicted a death blow to our national railways. Our railways do not carry any more freight; some stations are closed; shops are inactive; men are dismissed or suspended, and others have had their wages cut; and then the government is proud of that record of having reduced the expenditure on the Canadian National Railway. The government deserves as much credit for that reduction of expenditure as an inefficient and unsuccessful merchant deserves who, when he is on the verge of bankruptcy, dismisses his employees, closes some of his stores and buys no more goods. He also reduces his expenditures.
We have been told every session to wait. At the first session we were told to wait until the imperial conference took place in 1930. In the following session we were told to wait until the Ottawa conference took place. Then afterwards we were told to wait until the world economic conference took place. Well, it has taken place, and the best that can be said about this lasrt conference is that its failure did not cause the tremendous consequences which had been predicted that lack of success would hring about. Every statesman, everyone who had anything to do with that conference from the illustrious personality who opened it down to the humblest delegate, all stated that the strongest reason for the success of the conference was that the peoples of the world could not face the result of failure. But fortunately the breaking down of that conference does not seem to have been followed by anything more disastrous than what preceded it. We would be justified, however, in believing that sooner or later the world will suffer greater material harm if there is no international agreement as to trade, and if the nations do not begin to realize that they cannot all of them tiy to sell the same things in the same market at the same time. They must try to cooperate and exchange goods with one another and modify tariffs,, quotas, embargoes and so forth.
That conference served to emphasize in a most glaring manner what is 'the real trouble in almost every country in the world. On the first day the delegates were all unanimous as to the changes that had to be made. They all deplored the economic situation brought about by the policies of the individual countries. Secretary of State Hull, of the United States, summarized the evil in this way:
Economic nationalism as practised since the war comprises every single method of obstructing international capital and trade, such as 74726-33 i
high tariffs, quotas, embargoes, exchange restrictions and depreciated currencies.
Everybody seemed to agree that something must be done, but immediately after the real work started, the fight began so that the coming changes should not affect the respective countries of the delegates. The same condition exists in the national field. Everybody in Canada seems to admit the necessity of reforms, but those who seem to have most to do with the government of the country are not willing that those reforms should affect themselves or their respective industries.
The Prime Minister, of course, had disqualified himself from assuming any position of leadership in the promotion of needed reforms at the conference because as soon as he took office he summoned parliament for the purpose of erecting a wall around Canada, a wall of tariffs, high duties and embargoes. What moral authority could he have, then, to preach the return to economic sanity and cooperation? The Prime Minister now gives as his justification for his tariff policy of 1930 that we had then an unfavourable balance of trade, and that had to 'be changed. I do not, wish to express any opinion as to the merits or demerits of a favourable balance of trade, but I remember many hon. gentlemen opposite who said in my presence in this house that it did not mean anything. Further, during all the years when we had an overwhelmingly favourable balance of trade, the right hon. gentleman and his friends were just as vociferously clamouring for higher duties and higher protection in this house.
May I also say to the Prime Minister that what the people of this country are most anxious for is not a favourable balance of trade, so far as the trade of the country is concerned. What they do want is a favourable balance of trade in their own business, and that balance has been unfavourable because of the policies of the administration. The Prime Minister has been most unfortunate in translating patriotism into tariff barriers. In 1930 he erected that barrier of the tariff just before he went to the imperial economic conference, where he proposed to lower our tariff by ten per cent to the countries of the empire in exchange for a preference in the British market. But, of course, they all realized over there that when a wall is so high that it is impossible to get over it, it does not mean much to have it cut ten per cent if you cannot get over the wall even then. And that is why one of the fellow delegates of the Prime Minister qualified his proposal in a way which, in this parliament, we are too courteous to describe.
The Address-Mr. Lapointe

Following this we had the Ottawa conference. This conference has been described as a great achievement by the mover and seconder of the address. I consider it another link in the chain of harmful policies which are hampering world trade. As the right hon. gentleman had tied his hands in advance, before he went to the conference in 1930, so he tied his hands in advance, by the Ottawa agreement, before he went to the world economic conference of 1933. We have higher tariffs against all nations on a large number of articles, and he bound us by treaty not to change those tariffs, before entering into negotiations and common agreement with other nations.
In the Contemporary Review of January, 1934, Sir Archibald Sinclair gives the reasons why he has crossed the floor in the British House of Commons. At page 4 he says:
It is true that the economic situation remained grave, but in the Hew of the Liberal ministers it was being aggravated by the protectionist policy of the government, and from their standpoint the only possible justification for remaining in the government was the hope that the world economic conference would result in an, abatement of economic nationalism throughout the world and the restoration of world trade.
This hope, however, was impaired, if not destroyed, by the Ottawa agreements. If international trade was to be restored, one of the primary objectives which the British government were bound to pursue at the conference was the abolition of quotas which Mr. Runciman, the President of the Board of Trade, described at St. Ives on February 2, 1933, as "insane" and "the curse of European trade." Yet as a result of Ottawa we should be adopting quotas in this country at the very time when the Prime Minister, as chairman of the conference, would be appealing to other nations to relinquish theirs. Similar exhortations would be delivered by leading British ministers to foreign nations to lower their tariff walls: yet at the same time, as a result of Ottawa, large increases of British tariffs were in contemplation.
My right hon. friend can see therefore that we are not the only ones who deplore the trend that matters commercial have taken as a result of the Ottawa conference. My view is that economic imperialism as initiated by the Ottawa conference is not much better than economic nationalism as practised by the right hon. gentleman in 1930.
I am afraid that the forty minute rule will prevent me from saying all that I should like to say with respect to trade and similar matters in relation to the economic conference, because there is one question in particular on which I desire to say a word or two. I refer to the question of titles. I do not wish to discuss this matter at any length, but merely to defend the action of the House of Com-

mons of 1919 and to repel the charge of the Prime Minister that it was an affront to the King on the part of those who voted for that resolution. It is true that the resolution was not an act of parliament. The right hon. gentleman has built up a man of straw in order to knock him down when he says that only an act of parliament could abolish the prerogative. Nobody ever said that the prerogative did not exist; nobody ever said that this resolution of the House of Commons destroyed or abrogated the prerogative. It did not abolish it, nor was it intended to abolish 'it; it merely conveyed the will of the people of Canada, through their elected representatives, that this prerogative should not be exercised so far as Canada was concerned. The right hon. gentleman knows very well that, either by statute or by the conventional rules of the constitution, the King's prerogatives have been transferred to the ministry. Many people have queer ideas regarding the royal prerogative. In the exercise of the prerogative the crown acts on the advice of its ministers, who are responsible to parliament for the proper exercise of the authority. There is in fact no executive act of the crown for which some member of the ministry or the ministry collectively is not responsible. Things which the King formerly did by virtue of his prerogative he now does by virtue of the advice of those to whom the discretionary power has been transferred. And so, as Dicey states in his Law of the Constitution, eighth edition, page 421:
We may use the term "prerogative" as equivalent to the discretionary authority of the executive.
Ridges, in Constitutional Law of England, fourth edition, page 167, says:
The prerogative is no longer the personal prerogative of the king but the privilege of the executive.
Of course, everyone knows that honours are not bestowed by the King but by the Prime Minister. When His Majesty the King is mentioned in the resolution of 1919 it is His Majesty the King in the constitutional sense, namely, the authority that has discretionary power, the executive. I have no objection to the change which my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) is making in his resolution in order to meet the views of the Prime Minister and take away from him an excuse for opposing the resolution, but I still believe he was right in the way he had originally proposed it.
The Prime Minister suggested that his predecessors and those who were here in 1919 had no time to see his point because of

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
pressure of business. Let me tell him that the question was studied and considered and discussed for two consecutive sessions. A strong committee of the house was appointed and it sat for a long time. Strong men were on the committee, and the resolution was drafted as the result of the work of that committee. The resolution was voted for and approved by gentlemen who would not agree to anything which would have been an affront to the King. And I may say to my right hon. friend that there were men on this committee who would have been able to see whether or not there was an affront to His Majesty. The Hon. N. W. Rowell, present president of the Canadian Bar Association, was one of those who voted for the resolution, and he does not deserve the imputation conveyed in the words of the Prime Minister. So was the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, and he did not deserve this imputation. So was my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), so was my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. MoGibbon), and so were many others who voted on that resolution, as I did.

I can imagine the ranting which would have taken place in this house had my right bon. leader not done something to prevent the strike when he came back.

I was not in this house at that time. Had hon. gentlemen had the vision they could have connected up the Grand Trunk in the east with the Canadian Northern in the west, and we would have had a second transcontinental and probably no present day railway problems. When we remember that in connection with the third transcontinental the then leader of the Liberal party took the attitude that a railway from Moncton to the Pacific coast would cost $13,000,000, and when we couple with that the fact that the real cost of the railway-not to the Pacific coast at all, but from Moncton to Winnipeg-was $173,000,000, we cannot help but believe that hon. members opposite are the ones to blame for the railway problem which exists in Canada to-day.
When we come up to a more recent date, to 1929, a pre-election year, and learn that the right hon. gentleman and his party either permitted or forced the late management of the Canadian National railways to make commitments of $250,000,000 on hotels at Halifax and other places, on steamships, terminals, the purchasing of branch railway lines and the building of others-I say when we realize that they permitted or encouraged the management to make those commitments amounting to $250,000,000 in a pre-election year, when they passed around the railway pork barrel from coast to coast, we know that they should leave the railway question alone. We have had to clean up that mess, and we have cleaned it up.

The hon. member who has just taken his seat belittled our efforts. I say here, without fear of contradiction that anybody who knows what he is talking about will realize that we have saved the people of Canada about $15,000,000 per year in extravagant management which obtained under the late government, but which does not obtain to-day. I say, further, that the Canadian National railways are just as efficient to-day as they were when hon. members opposite went out of power. If I have ever in my life done any good work for my country it was when I helped to clean up that mess. We carried on and appointed the Duff commission. Then we appointed Mr. Fullerton, Mr. Morrow and Mr. Labelle to the railway board. I believe the railway history of this
The Address-Mr. Manion

government will stand the test of time far, far better than will the railway history of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Then, in regard to trade, the right hon. gentleman abused the present government. He compared the trade of to-day with that of a few years ago. He knows, of course, as well as does any other hon. member in the house, that the whole story of world trade is different to-day, that the trade of the world has gone down sixty per cent, and that the trade of Canada went down as did that of other countries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman also spoke of our trade with the United States. He forgets to mention that when he was Prime Minister of this country the United States were selling us two dollars worth of goods for every dollars worth that we sold them. In addition to that, they were putting up barriers against every line of goods we exported to them, particularly agricultural products. When we sat in opposition, as does the right hon. gentleman to-day, and suggested that the government of the day should retaliate, the only reply was that we must do nothing "to provoke" the United States. That was his attitude. While the Hawley-Smoot tariff was being put up against us and while the Fordney-McCumber tariff was working against our interests he sat quietly and said, "We must not provoke the United States." This government has dared to do that. We raised the tariffs where necessary. We treated the United States the way they treated us, and as a result we have the respect of that country. If there is to be a treaty made between this country and the United States I say that the government which has the respect of the United States would be the best government to bring it about.
I have only a few minutes left in which to speak, and in that time I shall sum up what I have said. May I point out that the truth of the whole matter is this-something which hon. members opposite do not choose to recognize when discussing present-day conditions-that the world has been going through four years of the most terrible depression it has ever known, and as a result Canada has suffered its share. There were

in industrial countries of the world 30,000.000 unemployed people. In the great rich republic to the south there were 12,000,000 or 13,000,000 unemployed. During that depression period many of the banks in the United States went into insolvency, but not one bank in Canada refused to pay one dollar to a depositor. Throughout the world debts were repudiated. Most of the European countries, if not all, have refused to pay interest on their debts, and some have refused to pay the capital. The South American republics were in the same position. Most of them are not paying interest on their bond debt, so that their bonds are selling at $6 and $7 that were originally purchased at $100. In Russia, that country which some of the bon. members in this house and elsewhere suggest we should copy, millions were starving, while not one person in Canada had to go without food, lodging or shelter-not one. That is the picture which hon. members opposite ignore. Not only did Canada share this condition, but we had such a drought throughout the western prairie provinces that as a result in Saskatchewan alone 300,000 men, women and children would not have been able to live without assistance from this government. They were carried through the winters of 1931 and 1932 by us. I say that no government and no country in the world could have prevented these conditions which were world wide. We had a crisis in the last four years which was just as great as the crisis of the great world war, and my right hon. friend was just as useful to us in this crisis as he was in the other. We have had no cooperation from him, no constructive advice. We have had only criticism, gloom and defeatism, and I should add, the offer of an election. It is often quoted against Marie Antoinette that shortly before the revolution when she was told that the people were crying for bread and could get none, she said, "Why don't they eat cake?" My right hon. friend in offering an election to the people at this time is suggesting something akin to the cake of Marie Antoinette.
Without doubt this government has faults and has made mistakes. We do not deny it. A government that does not make mistakes does not make anything, and a government that does not make mistakes in times like these would do nothing at ail, but I submit with all due respect to my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. La/pointe) who boasted so confidently that his party has the confidence of the people, that this country will not throw this government out to take his leader to lead them. I feel almost constrained to say

The Address-Mr. Marion
that before they would take the right hon. gentleman they would take the leader of the C.C.F. in the corner, and God knows they would have to be desperate to do that, Mr. Speaker.
What is the purpose of the right hon. gentleman's desire for an election at this time? It is for the purpose of capitalizing the discontent which exists and must exist at times like these not only in Canada but in every country of the world. That is the purpose, and his fear is that the country is going ahead and will continue to do so and get back to its path of progress and prosperity before an election takes place.
In brief, what is the record oif this government? During that time of crisis, which was as severe a crisis as the world war, we attempted in every way to relieve the conditions in many wavs by the construction of pulblic works in the beginning, and assisting the provinces, the municipalities and the railways to do likewise. We instituted camps for young unemployed homeless men. We have given loans to the prairie provinces, thereby saving the credit of those provinces, and in addition saving the credit of this dominion. We have saved the credit of the bonks and of the railways as well. We have given direct relief when we could do nothing else, and no one in this country has starved despite the fact that in Russia millions have starved. It has cost this country $160,000,000 to do these things. But that is not all.
This government put into effect the empire trade agreements, to the credit of my right hon. leader, which increased our trade with the empire last year by $37,000,000 as compared with the year before. We corrected the adverse trade balance which was affecting our exchange, and we have kept our place as fifth among the trading nations of the world, being outdistanced only by Great Britain, the United States, Germany and France. In addition, the Prime Minister settled a threatened railway strike, which I think was one of his major achievements, and much to his credit.
That is the record of this government, a record that is equalled, I think, by no other government in any other country in the world in these times. Canada has come out of this depression in at least as good a condition as any other country of the world with the possible exception of France up until a year ago. France profited by the fact that she was rebuilding her devastated territory, and she was able to hold out against the depression longer than any other country in the world, but France to-day is in difficulty.
In this country we have started on the upgrade. Every index points to it. The world is coming back to its own, and unless the so-called civilized countries of the world are so foolish as to go into another war, the world will shortly be back to where it should be, and Canada will be leading the way. Let us keep our heads. Let us keep steady. Let us as Canadians stand shoulder to shoulder in a time like this in an effort to put this country back on its proper track. This is not a time for demagogism, but a time for leadership, and after the leadership of this government carries Canada back, as it will, to normal conditions, then we will correct other evils. We will deal with such questions as unemployment insurance and planned economy, for I personally believe that we shall have to deal with these matters. But when your house is on fire you do not stop to argue about loans or taxes. The first thing you do is to put out the fire, leaving other matters to be dealt with later.
The Prime Minister has offered a program of public works, which, of course, cannot give employment to every unemployed man in this country, but remember that for every man who is given employment directly on public works, two or more men are also given employment indirectly.
So in conclusion I make this appeal to the whole house, that the whole house help Canada upon the upgrade at this time. Look about at the condition of the world. Look at France, at Austria; look at conditions in the West Indies and in the far east, and tell me, is this a time for partyism, for strife of that kind? I say that this is a time when we should stand side by side, when we should stop reviling our country, stop preaching pessimism, defeatism and gloom. It is a time when every hon. gentleman should stop attempting to hold back the progress of this country and should stand by us and help us in getting this country started on its way forward. We have weathered the worst economic hurricane that this world has ever known and it is our duty as Canadian citizens to endeavour to bring the ship of state into a safe harbour and then, after that is done, we can go back to party strife again if necessary.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the house
will permit me, even after the characteristically fiery and ebullient speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) to refer to a matter which he says, and I thoroughly agree with him, must be kept out of party politics. I want to say to my hon. friend and to this house that I am
The Address-Mr. Ralston

referring to it now because I consider, and I think he and the government will agree with me, that it is a matter which requires the early attention of this house and of the government, being what I regard as a serious injustice in connection with ex-service men that should be righted.
I preface my remarks by saying that I am not making it a matter of party politics. I agree thoroughly with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways in saying that this country should congratulate itself on the fact that the problems of the ex-service men have been dealt with by this House of Commons in a non-partisan manner. Time after time we have had committees of this house appointed, with strong partisans on both sides, and these committees have brought in unanimous reports in the interests of exservice men.
If the house will permit me for a moment, I want to bring to its attention a matter which I believe cannot stand without comment and which should be put upon record in order that the legislators gathered here may have a conception of what is going on in regard to the administration of the Pension Act in connection with the particular cases to which I refer.
I am calling attention to a practice which has grown up in the administration of the Board of Pension Commissioners whereby this board has assumed the right to determine the validity of marriages. I have a number of cases, but I shall mention only two or three. The situation is this:	A man has a
disability. He is pensioned for that disability. Under schedule A of the Pension Act, if he is married he gets additional pension on account of his wife, and if he has children he gets further additional pension on account of the children. The Board of Pension Commisisoners within the last year or two at least-I do not know whether this practice existed before-have instituted the practice of ascertaining whether or not the soldier who happens to be getting a pension was previously married or whether his wife was previously married, and if that is the case the board has required definite legal evidence that the previous spouse, either of the husband or of the wife, as the case may be, was dead at the time of the marriage or is dead now. That practice is different from the practice in the courts of this country. In the courts of this country there is a presumption that if a person is not heard of for seven years, by persons with whom he or she would likely be in communication, and if inquiry has been made un-
successfully to locate such person, that person is dead. Under the criminal laws of this country a man or a woman cannot be convicted of bigamy for marrying believing that the former spouse is dead, even if seven years have not elapsed; and if seven years have elapsed, then the onus is on the crown to prove that the former spouse has in fact been heard of. Now what has the Board of Pension Commissioners been doing? I will give three cases by way of illustration.
First I will cite the case of a man with a disability-gunshot wound in the arm, fracture of both bones, arm deeply scarred, through and through bullet wound in the thigh. This man is receiving a 55 per cent pension, which entitles him to $37.50, and having a wife and six children he is entitled to an additional sum of $42, making in all $79.50. The board discovered that this man had been previously married. The circumstances were these. He was married in 1917 and lived with his wife for one week, after which time she deserted him, moving away to Toronto, and he had not since heard of or from her. He signed what he thought were papers which, as he believed, completely annulled the marriage, and in 1923 he was married again by a Protestant clergyman in Nova Scotia. With the wife of this second marriage he has lived ever since, and they have six children. They are recognized in the community as man and wife, are moral and respectable in every particular, and yet the Board of Pension Commissioners, upon finding out about the previous marriage, sent him in effect a bill for $3,000 for the money they had paid him on account of this second wife and the children, taking the view that this marriage was bigamous and that the children are consequently illegitimate. They have sent him a bill for $3,000, saying to him, "Until you pay us back to the full that $3,000 we shall not pay you one cent of the $37.50 pension." That is the practice in this particular case.

I have in my hand the letter of the Board of Pension Commissioners, in which they say:
As the statute makes no provision for the payment of additional pension for an illegal wife or for illegitimate children the board had no alternative but to cancel the allowances from date of award.
In other words, the Board of Pension Commissioners, sitting in their judicial capacity, simply bastardized these children and declaring the marriage bigamous, without affording the man an opportunity to present his case. His pension is out off and afterwards, if he wishes, he can make representations.
The second case is that of the wife of an ex-soldier. She was married in Ireland in 1884 and lived with her husband a year, when he deserted her. She never heard from him and believed-in fact was told-that he had died in the United States; and seventeen years afterwards she married another man in Scotland. This man is now refused a pension on account of his wife because forsooth the Board of Pension Commissioners say that there is no proof of the death of the woman's former husband, notwithstanding that the common law, as the Prime Minister and other lawyers in the house know, presumes under such circumstances that the previous spouse is dead.
The third case is perhaps the most serious, that of a man with hip amputation. This man was married in 1906 and his wife deserted him. He pursued inquiries for fifteen years but could not find her; he had no word of her. He got an order from the chief justice of a court of one of the provinces in this dominion that the first wife was presumed to be dead. Yet the Board of Pension Commissioners has reduced the pension of this man with a leg off at the hip. He was getting, I believe, something like S99 and they have taken all but $5.31 a month in order to repay what they say was an illegal payment of pension.
I mention these cases because in my opinion they are matters that should be taken up immediately by the house. I know that the government has them under consideration now, but the point is that time is running and these cases are urgent. They are all quite old, and still no action is taken by the board. I can only say that in cases of this kind, where good faith is shown, where people marry believing that they have the right to do so, and perform the duties of husband and wife, raising children and supporting them, the country, to say the least, should not fine
them if something is discovered to be wrong with their marriage. The state should not take away under these circumstances what had already been paid, particularly when the Pension Act, under section 2 (c), recognizes that "children" includes illegitimate children, and when the act in another section recognizes that a widow, even though there has been no proper marriage service, was the wife of the man concerned for the purposes of pension. The rule of the board is harsh and unjust and remedial measures should be taken in connection with this matter.

I am afraid I cannot attempt to follow the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) in the peregrinations of his speech, but I will deal as I proceed with a few of the points he made. He did not answer, as I thought he would, my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) with regard to titles, and it seemed to me that the criticism which was made by the hon. member for Quebec East to the effect that the Prime Minister had taken an hour and a half mouthing legal technicalities in connection with a matter that does not present

any legal difficulties but is purely a question of policy, as to whether the wishes of the people's representatives in this country were to be observed, was a subject to which the right hon. gentleman might have given more attention. Let me tell him now what happened with regard to the administration of these roads under governments of
which he was a supporter and under Liberal governments. First take the amount earned by this system of roads and available for all interest; from 1919 to 1921 there was nothing whatever available, but there was an average deficit of $22,000,000 yearly. From 1922 to 1930 there was an average surplus of $24,000,000 per annum. For 1931 there was a deficit again of $5,000,000; I have not the figures for 1932. Secondly, I make the same comparison, after paying interest to the public: from 1919 to 1921 the annual deficit was $53,000,000. We have improved, and I hope sincerely that we may keep on improving. But what my hon. friends have not told us yet is what they have done to bring about that improvement. That is the real question. They have done everything possible to cripple trade and increase the taxes in this country. They speak about the Ottawa agreements, and I am going to deal with those in a moment, but I have not seen any trade arrangement made by this government which has perceptibly accelerated the normal increase of trade which has taken place in all the countries of the world.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways spoke of wholesale prices. Well, in wholesale prices I think he will find very little comfort, because the United States is considerably ahead of us in regard to increases in wholesale prices. But my hon. friend just tosses that to one side and says, "We have increased wholesale prices." Of course we have; let us take what comfort we can out of it, but there is not much credit to the government in that fact. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister put on Hansard the increase in steel production since the beginning of 1933, but the percentage of increase in the United States was far greater, and that jumble of figures which he put on Hansard and which appears at pages 75 to 79 fails to show anything which any reasonable man could say was done by the present government to assist in producing any increase.

Then my right hon. friend spoke about the increase in Canadian exports to Great Britain since the spring of this year. We are glad there is an increase, but does my right hon. friend realize that the pound, which was $3.84 last January, had risen to $5.09 in December, and that the buying power of the pound in the Canadian market was increased accordingly? Naturally under those circumstances the British people would buy more from the Canadian market. Does my right hon. friend realize that conditions have improved in Great Britain, which surely ought to have something to do with the increase in exports by the Dominion of Canada to the old country? That was not mentioned at all. On reading the Prime Minister's speech one would think that the sole cause of this increase was the Ottawa agreements fostered by himself and his government.
Then my hon. friend the Minister of Railways said that imports from the United States had decreased perceptibly. That is quite so, but is that a matter for comfort? Is that a matter for congratulation? Generally speaking our imports from the United States are producers' goods and producers' equipment, goods which we use in manufacturing, and if our imports go down it means that our industrial activity has been curtailed by just that much. If my hon. friend will look at the trade returns for 1932 he will find that 65 per cent of all our imports from the United States were producers' goods and producers' equipment, or in other words things we needed to work with or work on. In those things our imports have gone down considerably, but I do not regard it as a matter for congratulation at all; it seems to me that decreased imports of raw material and of equipment simply mean that our national activities have declined. If we do not import that material it means that our producing industries have slackened accordingly.

I suggest that what my right hon. friend opposite really does as he goes to bed at night-and I hope he will not accuse me of being blasphemous-is to fall on his knees and thank God for Roosevelt, thank God for Great Britain and thank God for a situation around us whereby our condition is being stabilized, and improved notwithstanding the inaction of this government. All they do is to tell us to tighten our belts, to remember the traditions of our forefathers, to have patience; and may I add that the people of Canada are getting mighty tired of it. This government has done its best to discourage industry, so far as primary producers are concerned. For example, let us consider the fishermen. The duties on
The Address-Mr. Ralston

gasoline, on oiled clothing, on rubber boots, on food, and on many other commodities have been increased, and there is the tax on sugar. Everything has been made more expensive, but the fishermen has to sell in an unprotected market and at the same time has to beg this government for a little relief -not a big amount-a little relief, in the way of small public works and facilities in order that he may be able to pursue his calling in comparative-and only comparative-safety. Imagine a fisherman out on the Atlantic in this winter weather following his vocation in order to make new W'ealth for Canada and paying increased taxes on the things he uses and at the same time getting little consideration from this government when he asks for comparatively insignificant assistance which would help him in connection with his work.
I say to you this, Mr. Speaker,-and this is my last word-notwithstanding the fact that my right lion, friend's promises have been unfulfilled, notwithstanding the increase in taxation, notwithstanding the tremendous increase in debt, notwithstanding the broken pledges regarding employment, notwithstanding the banders which have been placed in the way of trade, notwithstanding the handicaps under which this government has placed this dominion, Canada is coming through, and we all are profoundly thankful for it, but I say it is not because of, but in spite of the administration of the present government.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has pictured the ship of state. The ship of state is manned by a crew scared to do anything; they are so fearful that they will not even touch the sails. They say, "Be cautious, be careful." They are even afraid to stand by the wheel and steer a definite course. They cannot even make up their minds to avail themselves of the auxiliary power. Canadians, the passengers, say to them, "For heaven's sake do something and get us out of the storm." This crew's only reply is, "Be patient, the storm is passing." But suddenly the captain has a bright idea; he says, "There is something we can do; there is a bronze tablet on the companion way with the names of the great and the illustrious on it. Let us polish up the bronze tablet." That is the best he can do in the way of seamanship. What I mean is that the right hon. gentleman does not attempt to tackle and solve the pressing problems for the welfare of the Canadian people but busies himself instead with the matter of titles.
I submit that this government has done at least one thing: it has proved Canada's inherent soundness, because a country which can weather the conditions of the past three

or four years with a government like the one sitting opposite to manage its affairs need have no fear for the future.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with previous speakers in this debate in extending my very sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address. Unfortunately _ at the commencement of all our sessions the leaders of all parties in the house find it necessary to pay tribute to those who have passed the great divide since the house prorogued. May I in a very humble way this evening be permitted, sir, in this house to try to express the great loss which the Dominion of Canada has sustained since last we parted on account of the death of that great and distinguished Canadian, Sir Arthur Currie. I think, sir, that I am voicing the sentiments of every hon. member on the floor of this house when I say, without at all presuming to add to the marvelous tributes that have been paid to his memory, that he was great in war, great in peace, and great indeed in the heart of his country. May I also be permitted to place upon Hansard a quotation from one of his recent speeches, because it deals with a subject which I intend to present to the house this evening, and which has already been

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
referred to by two of the speakers this afternoon:
Our hope in war was to salvage the old moral values of civilization. Our hope in peace when we came home was to use our influence and strength for the placing of our country on a little higher plane.
Our determination was to see that our broken comrades-the shattered wreckage of the war [DOT]-and the dependents of our dead comrades should never want nor suffer need. Our intention was to prove to our country that grief and hate were not the only results of the courage and the death of ten million men but that mutual help and service and sacrifice were still alive in our country.
I desire, Mr. Speaker, to use those words by way of a preliminary towards the consideration, of a discussion in regard to pensions, but before I pass along, may I refer by the way with the utmost commendation to the appointment made yesterday, I understand by the government of the new Sergeant-at-Arms of this house. I think that appointment reflects great credit upon this administration, that it is one of the finest appointments they have made during the last four years, and I commend that appointment very heartily.
My honourable, temperamental and rodomontade friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), speaking din the bouse this afternoon, had the supreme, the sublime yet customary effrontery to say that I had suggested the injection of the pensions question into the arena of party politics. I think, Mr. Speaker, that my bon. friend has forgotten my attitude in this house during the last three and a half years. He surely must have forgotten my attitude on this question last year in this house. If he had only consulted his own colleagues in the administration I am sure he would have been told that when the pensions question was before this house last year I assisted the hon. Minister of Pensions (Mr. MacLarein) in piloting that legislation through this house in a non-partisan way when there was some criticism coming from my own side of the house. So I want to tell my hon. friend the Minister of Railways that I resent and I repudiate the suggestion that he made. In my experience in this house in the last three and a half years he is the only one, Mr. Speaker, that has ever suggested or insinuated that any hon. member of this house had ever endeavoured to bring the question of pensions into the arena of party politics.

All that
I said at Fort William I am going to repeat
on the floor of this house to-night-every single word'-and if my hon. friend will not agree with my conclusions when I am through, then' I shall be glad to withdraw anything that I said at Fort William or here to-night.
May I be permitted the indulgence of the house very briefly indeed to traverse the history of pensions legislation in this dominion?
In the first place, after the armistice we had the appointment of the Board of Pension Commissioners, with their exclusive jurisdiction, with no right of appeal to any body existing, with the statutory appointment of the commissioners for ten years, and with ministers of the crown having no authority whatsoever over the board, and with the right of decision retained by the commissioners sitting here in Ottawa. We recall the widespread dissatisfaction that existed in the dominion. We had parliamentary committee after parliamentary committee appointed from the floor of this house, and eventually we had that royal commission presided over by my distinguished and able colleague the hon. member for Shelburme-Yarmouth (Mr. Hairston) which considered the whole question in the year 1922. As a result of their recommendations, in the first place, that some form of appeal tribunal should be set up, in the second place that an opportunity should be provided for the appearance of the applicant before the body making the final decision, we bad set up in 1923 the federal appeal board.
We had further dissatisfaction existing throughout the dominion, coming down to the appointment of the special committee appointed by this house in 1929-30 and presided over by my hon. friend the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). As a result of the recommendations of the latter committee we had established in this country the pension tribunals system, numbering twelve, with wide powers of jurisdiction, with an extensive pensions advocate system being set up, with commission counsel appointed to represent the state, with automatic reference to the pension tribunals of many cases, and the establishment of a final court, the pension appeal court. There must be a recasting of this whole question, in my humble judgment, as was done in Australia, by a combination of voluntary and compulsory conversion. There must be a writing down of interest rates on public and private obligations all across the Dominion of Canada. That is the only way that we can meet the question of unemployment. We have had suggestions from our friends to the left in regard to shorter hours; I agree with them. We have had resolutions in regard to unemployment insurance; I agree with that. We have had various schemes to remedy unemployment, but in my judgment we can never cure the unemployment situation that prevails to-day until we solve two great problems, the problem of our trade and the problem of finance. In my humble judgment those two great questions are indissolubly intertwined. Some hon. members believe that the tariff affords a panacea for all our troubles. There are others, sitting to my left, who believe that monetary reform is the panacea for all our troubles. I agree with the remarks made by Lionel D. Edie in his great book on banking and credit, in which he says that the economic theories of the industrial equilibrists dovetail into those of the school of monetary reform. The trouble with Canada has been that both major parties have been deliberately directing their trade policies towards the empire-and I am not criticizing or complaining of that-but the financial policies of this dominion have been linked with the 
great republic to the south. Canada must Wake up to the fact that financial policies and industrial policies cannot be kept separate. It is one of the important functions of governments in the future to recognize that these two must be linked up. A solution of our unemployment problem is impossible until we have arrived at the answer to these two great questions.
We have had discussed also the question of note issue and metallic coverage. Two years ago in this house I suggested action on this subject, and it is strange to find now so many reformers in the house, on both sides, who were not so keen on these ideas two years ago, but who are so ready to proclaim these theories to-day, when the government is facing defeat and disaster before the country. In regard to the note issue, the view of some of the best economists, including John Maynard Keynes and the English Macmillan committee, is that a metallic coverage is not necessary for internal currency. Even at the world economic conference they reduced the required metallic coverage from forty per cent to twenty-five per cent for external obligations. The Macmillan committee went further and assessed the scientific basis for a managed currency as one-fifth of the bank deposits. In Canada this would be one-fifth of $2,000,000,000, or $400,000,000, leaving the way open, in my judgment, for a safe addition to our present note issue of over $200,000,000. That is without considering at all the appreciation in value of our present gold reserve. So I say that instead of drifting idly and uselessly as this administration is doing, it should be facing these questions of our financial structure, our public debt, our interest obligations, and a comprehensive public works program.

Others say that we have raised it to the point of prohibition. Well, here are the facts. The average rate of duty on all goods for the fiscal year 1929-30 was, under the general tariff 15.51 per cent; treaty tariffs, 28.56 per cent; British preferential, 14.1,1 per cent. I wish to turn for a moment to the question of our trade. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that we have lost our trade, that our trade has been dissipated. I have here some rather interesting figures, given by the chief statistician of the League of Nations, which show the fall in world trade. In 1929 world trade amounted to $68,641,000,000; in 1930, to $55,575,000,000; in 1931, to $39,769,000,000; and in 1932 it had fallen to $26,611,000,000. That is the gauge, Mr. Speaker, of the trend of world conditions, and that is the gauge that should be applied to Canadian trade in order to interpret correctly whether or not Canada is suffering unduly in comparison with the rest of the world. My hon. friends, of course, in their party enthusiasm, brush aside all these considerations. They charge us with responsibility for the loss of trade. They totally ignore the fall in the price level throughout the world. I shall show in a moment the volume increase in our trade which I think is very encouraging. But whether we like this government and its policies or not, common decency and fairness demand that we measure the trend of Canadian trade by comparison with the trend of trade throughout the world. What if in 1930 we did have, as everybody had, expectations and hopes that the depression then under way, or the depression which was under way before we took office, would not last as long as it did? Is that a deplorable thing? I remember in the early days of the war how nearly everybody said that it would be over by Christmas of 1914; and there was just an odd person or two who said that it would last a year or two. Lord Kitchener was looked upon as a base pessimist for prophesying that it would last three or four years. But it lasted longer than anyone dreamed of; and so when we entered this depression in the fall of 1929, when the great collapse of the New York stock market occurred and precipitated the period of depression the general opinion throughout the
world was that one year, or peradventure eighteen months, would see the end of the depression, as we had seen other cycles pass in years gone by. But all over the world without exception the depression continued to get deeper and deeper.
Someone referred this afternoon to Great Britain emerging from the depression earlier than we have. That is true, but Great Britain [DOT]was in the trough of the depression for some years before we entered it; and that ought to be remembered. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth was not very fair when he made a point of Great Britain emerging in advance of this country or making more rapid progress, if you like to put it that way, because he ignored entirely the effect upon this country, as upon other countries, of Great Britain's going off the gold standard. I am not questioning the right or the wisdom of that step. As a matter of fact, I belong to that school of thought that believes she was right, but the effect was terrific throughout the world. I do not think that any economist up to the present time has ever properly gauged its effect upon the world. That is a fact over which we had no control and no possibility of control.
Then again there was the economic collapse of virtually all the countries of Europe, as I shall be able to show. My hon. friend points out that Britain is a little in advance of us in recovery, and I glory in the fact; I think it is splendid. But it is due partly to their farsightedness as statesmen and partly to the following of those careful and cautious policies which characterize Mr. Chamberlain as Chancellor of the Exchequer. And may I say to my hon. friend that the Prime Minister has been charged with walking step by step with Neville Chamberlain, the very gentleman who is responsible for the conditions in Great Britain which the hon. member opposite lauded this afternoon. In other words, he condemns the Prime Minister of Canada for following the same policy.

speechtext: Would the minister tell us the difference between buying futures and gambling in them?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend
knows quite well, as do many other hon. members, that were it not for the purchasers of future contracts on the Winnipeg or *Chicago market, as the case may be, it would not be possible to market in orderly fashion the western wheat crop. No one knows that better than does the western farmer; but it is quite true that the purchaser of future contracts, whether in Chicago, Winnipeg or elsewhere, may be a speculator in wheat. Who
li 52
The Address-Mr. Stevens

buy future contracts? First, the millers for their future use, because millers will buy in October or November for delivery in May or July. That is their regular practice. They thus ensure a certain amount for their requirements. Exporters, in anticipation of their requirements, purchase futures. Futures are purchased for the Scottish Cooperative, which is one of the biggest organizations. Purchasers for the big milling interests in Great Britain, Bunge, Dreyfus, the great dealers on the European continent, all buy futures for delivery at some future date. I am reminded that the Stamp commission which went into this whole question made a decision-and it was accepted-which was distinctly in favour of those who had wheat to sell, namely, the producers. It is vital to the producer of *wheat in the prairie provinces that when his time of delivery in the fall comes, there should be some agency available to absorb the excess of wheat that is offered for sale, and that is all that has been done. If there were no buyer there would be no sale. My hon. friend knows that had Mr. McFarland, the head of the pool selling agency, refused to take up in the fall of 1932 and again this autumn, the excess delivery over purchases by the mills and the exporters, there would have been a wholly disastrous slump in the price of wheat beyond any point to which it actually went. Last fall I pointed out all these facts [DOT]to some hon. gentlemen opposite. Would tny hon. friends now say: You have been gambling in wheat; why have you not come out into the open? Anybody who knows (anything about business knows that if a government were to disclose its hand day by day in regard to these things, it would have ruined the wheat market. There is not a single dealer in wheat, whether he is a producer, or a representative of the pools, or any of the purchasing or selling agencies, but would tell any hon. gentleman that what I have just stated is true. It would have ruined the market.
We have been faced in Europe with quotas, with high rates of duty for which we were not responsible, which were in existence before We took office. Faced with these conditions, not because we have closed markets, we have done everything that ingenuity, skill, foresight and the backing of the government could do to hold the wheat market of Canada steady in the interests of the producers.
I should like to have dealt with a few other questions, but I shall not infringe upon the time of the house. In conclusion let me say this: this is the situation in our great markets, namely, Great Britain and the continent.

Fortunately Great Britain now gives us a 'sheltered market due to our agreement, but in the great European markets of France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Holland, Norway, Sweden, Czechoslovakia and so on, due to the disturbed conditions which have obtained in the last few years, unfortunately for us, as well as for others, systems of quotas and high rates of duty obtain, but we hold with the governments of those countries the most friendly relations. I do not know of any of them that are not on the most friendly terms and I am hopeful that as time goes by and as conditions improve, those markets will be an increasing source of absorption of Canadian products.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this debate closes, I wish to briefly discuss the financial and economic situation of the country, such as it appears to me. I disagree, sir, with the views expressed by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. To restore prosperity to this country one must, first, desire it, and the government certainly does not. Is it by its policy of indifference or by its exaggerated policy of protection that we shall succeed in restoring prosperity? Prosperity, under the Conservative regime, is like a flower which hardly blossoms, and hon. gentlemen on the government benches must know that they cannot coax it, they must show themselves worthy of it and deserve it. Can we hope that prosperity will be restored to this country?
I fear that we shall never see it again. We shall certainly not prosper before we can improve our situation, federal, provincial or municipal, and put our financial affairs on a sound footing, and, so to speak, make an inventory of the country's finances.
I contend, sir, that we must first know how we stand, salvage the ship of state which is sinking. I, moreover, state, as we are all aware, that Canada will soon be bankrupt. Very soon we shall have to repudiate our liabilities or default, unless we act immediately. Where is the so called government policy of sound money leading us to, where has it led us hitherto? What do the government's followers think of the labour situation? What do they think of the labourer without work who toils for a pittance? The representatives of the counties adjacent to the Quebec district understand what I mean by a labourer working for a pittance. They are numerous in their counties and I wonder why they have

The Address-Mr. Lacroix
not protested hitherto. The farmer, unable to obtain credit, is forced to leave his farm and seek another home on new land. The country merchant has lost 60, 80 and 90 per cent of his stock; the manufacturer, in certain industries, is on the road to ruin. For instance, in the paper industry, 56 per cent of the companies are bankrupt or reorganizing.
The figures which I shall quote, sir, will exactly describe the situation of municipalities, provinces, and Canada as a whole; it will, perhaps, impress many of us who are wondering where we are bound for and when the ship will become stranded? In 1911, the national debt amounted to $340,042,052; in 1921, $2,340,878,984; in 1930, $2,177,763,959; in 1080, $2,599,089,000. While in 1038, the dominion debt for the guarantee of railway bonds-less the $60,000,000 lately guaranteed to the Canadian Pacific Railway-amounted to $996,148,000. In 1930, the provincial liabilities amounted to $1,363,382,000. In 1933 also, indirect liabilities amounted to $215,977,000. In 1933, municipality liabilities had reached $1,584,000,000. The total debt of Canada in 1933, including railway guarantees, not including, however, the $60,000,000 guaranteed to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but including the provincial and municipal liabilities, amounted to the fabulous sum of $6,758,596,000 or $651.33 per capita.
According to the figures I have just quoted, the total debt of Canada between 1930 and 1934 has increased $1,167,236,444. That comprises all the dominion, provincial and municipal liabilities, namely, a yearly increase of $291,809,111 or $29.08 per capita, by which we aggravate the situation of this country.
To better analyse and understand this extraordinary state of things, I took the pains of looking up the United States's national debt and comparing it with ours, seeing that the United States government's policy is striving to wipe out its domestic debt. I find that in the United States on June 1, 1933, the federal, state and municipal governments, including county councils, had a total debt of $42,223,249,000 or $355.10 per capita. In Canada our debt amounts to $651.33 per capita compared with $355.10 in the United States. This means that every Canadian owes the double of what the United States citizen owes. Moreover, the United States have no outside debts, while ours amounts to 40 per cent of the total debt.
Recently, at Vancouver, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) drew the attention of his audience to this fact. In Toronto, he stated that Canada's credit
could not be further extended. In Montreal, he attributed our colossal debt to railway construction. To my mind the responsibility rests not alone on railways, but mostly on the public men who then voted these guarantees to railways. The government in office in 1911, 1912, and 1913, of which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was a supporter, voted on many an occasion subsidies and guarantees to the Canadian Northern, owned by MacKenzie and Mann; and I could point out many instances where our Prime Minister himself approved these subsidies and guarantees to that railway. In 1914, according to Hansard, did he not state himself that in 1912 and 1913, he had approved of these subsidies? I simply wish to show that if the country's liabilities have reached this colossal figure, all must shoulder their own responsibility and not place the burden on Sir Wilfrid Laurier's administration.
Another event which we have not forgotten and which is the cause of our present plight, is the great war with its enormous waste. One well recalls the memorable speech of the right hon. Mr. Meighen in the course of which he exclaimed, "To the last man and to the last dollar!" Well, sir, the last dollar is gone and no one wants to be reminded of it.

The hon.
member does not seem disposed, this evening, to settle Canada's debt.
If we desire prosperity in this country, we must first put our house in order and make use of stringent means which the situation demands. Why not forsake this policy of sound money and increase the purchasing power of our people? If the United States have found it necessary to deflate their dollar to 59 cents, and soon to 50 cents, when their debt per capita amounts to only $335-10, why should we, in Canada, strive to liquidate our debt with money of fictitious value and which would not be acceptable to our people?
If the United States find it necessary to stabilize their dollar at 50 cents, and if our liabilities amount to double what theirs are, I state that the par value of the Canadian dollar should be 50 per cent of the value of the United States dollar; namely that we should stabilize our dollar at half of its present value.
Moreover, other countries have set the example. In 1920, France made an inventory of her assets and studied the paying power of her people and came to the conclusion that to honourably meet her liabilities she had to stabilize her franc at 3-92 cents, namely, 19^ cents on the dollar. Great Britain also resorted to deflation on the pound sterling. Sweden, Norway, Italy, Belgium, Japan and many other countries were forced to deflate their currency so as to meet their liabilities.
It may be asked-that is, perhaps, what the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) wishes to find out-How shall we meet our liabilities abroad? We can do so, if we wish. Canada ranks second among gold producing countries. According to the Bureau of Statistics, in 1933, we produced $60,880,000 worth of gold, reckoning its value at $20.67 an ounce. However, if it is appraised at market value, namely $35 an ounce, the gold production in our country, in 1933, amounted to $103,077,450. Why not fund this foreign debt at fifty years and pay it with the products of our gold mines, and not by crediting the capitalist with a premium on gold as we are at present doing, leaving the impression that we are very wealthy.
Recently the United States revalued all their gold and the government alone were credited with the profits. Even on gold held in reserve by the United States national banks,

the premiums was credited to the government and not to these banks. I wonder why we should pay the premium to gold producers in this countiy instead of crediting it to the government.
We could, sir, utilize another natural resource in order to liquidate our liabilities. The means which I shall suggest may not please every one; however, when one wishes to pay his debts, all legitimate means are resorted to. I refer to gasoline and oils sold in Canada. According to last year's statistics, we consumed 503,800,000 gallons of gasoline. Two years ago the consumption amounted to 100,000,000 gallons more. Why permit this gasoline to be sold from 7 to 10 cents more, per gallon, than it should sell? Who benefits by it? Who are those who are benefited by this 7 to 10 cents margin over and above the cost price? The profits in such a transaction go to Rockefeller, the Standard Oil of New Jersey, the Imperial Oil of Canada, a subsidiary company and other oil companies which are connected with and owned by the Imperial Oil Co. of Canada.
In April last, the Standard Oil and the PanAmerican Oil submitted to me a price for a cargo of gasoline; I wish to quote their figures in order that they may appear in Hansard. For a cargo of gasoline loaded in the Gulf of Mexico, the Standard Oil and Pan-American Oil asked me 3-25 cents per gallon. The transportation company charged 35 cents per barrel for this shipment from the Gulf of Mexico to Quebec, or 0-82 cents per gallon, a total of 4-07 cents per American gallon, delivered in Quebec. Comparing the United States gallon with that of Canada, the latter contains one fifth more. Therefore, in April last, the large United States trusts, owners of the Imperial Oil and other Canadian companies, asked me 4-89 cents for an Imperial gallon, delivered on board ship in the port of Quebec.
What was, then, the sale price of gasoline on tank cars, at Quebec and Montreal? I inquired and found that the Imperial Oil and the Champlain Oil, were selling gasoline at 1-2-5 cents per gallon, at Montreal and that the shipping cost from Montreal to Quebete amounted to 2-5 cents per gallon-

Why tolerate such a situation in Canada and thus permit the removal of $50,300,000 of the people's savings, because a group of men known as the gasoline trust are benefited by an exaggerated protection.
This proves how shameful are the profits of the gasoline trust in Canada. Last summer, as you are probably aware, tourists, at Lasalle, Quebec, could only purchase three gallons of gasoline for $1, while, across the border, at Plattsburg, they obtained six gallons for the same price. Yet we do not bestir ourselves when the public debt increases $29.08 per capita yearly! If it is desired that the Canadian people should continue to pay top prices for their gasoline, why not levy an excise tax of 10 cents per gallon? Let us do away with tariff barriers and permit outsiders to sell their gasoline in this country. We shall then soon find out that gasoline will sell less than 30 cents per gallon, even including this aforesaid excise tax and those levied by provincial governments.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it would somewhat be a great sacrifice for this government to turn against trusts, especially the gasoline trust, the Standard Oil and Imperial Oil. That is why I wanted to explain our financial and economic situation such as I see it and to suggest certain remedies.

Is the increase of $11,504,428 in exports a compensation for a decrease of $309,991,661 in British and foreign exports on those Canadian products?
Home consumption year 1932-33 compared with 1930-31
Dressed beef, 89,161,967 pounds less; sheep and lamb, 4,845,080 pounds more; leather, $18,318,887 less; dairy products, 20,841,926 pounds less; peas, 973,616 bushels less; potatoes, 2,284,769 hundredweight less; fish products, $21,847,107 less; grain, 89,403,558 bushels less; wheat flour, 1,689,000 barrels less.
Sir, it is pretty hard for the house to understand the full meaning of figures read so hastily, until they appear in Hansard, but I wish to conclude thus. I have in my hand a book written by a very distinguished member of the press gallery, Mr. Leopold Richer. It is entitled Marche de Dupes? or A Fool's Bargain? This is the only way to describe the agreements of the Ottawa conference. I will say no more, I leave the figures to speak for themselves. I do not wish to offend anyone but lit is a crime to burn incense before the right hon. Prime Minister by telling him that his policy has been a success, when taking one by one the summaries he has given to the house we prove that they mean not only a loss in exports but also a decrease in home consumption. The facts are there; what I have said is not based on imagination; it is not a tale I have told to the house, I have obtained the figures of exports and imports from the bureau of statistics. I have worked on them for three or four days; now I hope there are some gentlemen on the other side of the house who will tell the Prime Minister that he has shot his bolt and it is time for him to remove himself gently from the picture. We might wait another year, for an election- provided that the Conservative party and the government select another leader-and try the administration for a year longer under that new leadership.
Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by Mr. Gardiner, that the following words be added to the motion:
We respectfully regret that Your Excellency's present advisers have not taken such steps as are necessary to deal adequately with unemployment, to reduce the burden imposed by the public debt, and to put the agricultural industry on a basis that will ensure to the farmer a decent standard of living.
The position of a third group in the house is a somewhat difficult one. If we vote nonconfidence in the government it may be interpreted as indicating that we have confidence in the official opposition. But such is not the

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
case. Hence the subamendment which we introduced at an earlier stage of the debate, which however, was declared out of order. We now seek to place our position before the house.
May I point out that when we vote against the government we do not necessarily reject or disapprove of all the measures mentioned in the speech from the throne. We recognize that there are some good measures indicated in that speech, some things that we may approve. When the legislation is actually brought down and we understand more fully the details of it we may be inclined to vote for certain measures proposed in that speech. But on the whole we feel that the proposals are altogether inadequate to meet the situation with which we find ourselves confronted at the present time. Hence while we join with the official opposition in voting for their amendment, we now put forward our own amendment, and possibly they may reciprocate by voting for it.
